topics.title: Decimals and place value
topics.hook: Each place is worth ten times the place to its right: hundreds, tens, ones . tenths, hundredths, thousandths.
topics.teach: Explain why 0.4 is bigger than 0.35 even though it has fewer digits.
topics.talk: Ask her which is bigger, 0.5 or 0.45, and why.

topics.title: Negative numbers
topics.hook: Below zero, the bigger the digit, the colder it is: −8 is less than −3.
topics.teach: Explain what subtracting a negative number does.
topics.talk: If it is −3°C and gets 5 degrees warmer, what is the temperature?

topics.title: Fractions on a number line
topics.hook: The denominator is down: it says how many equal parts; the numerator on top counts how many you take.
topics.teach: Explain how you find where 3/4 goes on a number line.
topics.talk: Ask her where 5/4 goes on a ruler that is 2 long.

topics.title: Comparing fractions
topics.hook: The bigger the denominator, the smaller the slice: 1/8 of a pizza is less than 1/5.
topics.teach: Explain why 1/8 is smaller than 1/5.
topics.talk: Would she rather have 2/3 or 3/5 of a pizza? Why?

topics.title: Equivalent fractions and simplifying
topics.hook: Whatever you do to the top, do to the bottom.
topics.teach: Explain how you simplify a fraction.
topics.talk: Ask her to simplify 12/16 in her head.

topics.title: Adding and subtracting fractions
topics.hook: Same bottoms first: only add slices of the same size, then add the tops. Never add the denominators.
topics.teach: Explain why you can’t just add the denominators.

topics.title: Multiplying and dividing fractions
topics.hook: Multiply the tops, multiply the bottoms. To divide: keep it, change it, flip it.
topics.teach: Explain why multiplying by a fraction smaller than 1 makes a number smaller.
topics.talk: What is half of a quarter?

topics.title: Fractions of amounts
topics.hook: Divide by the bottom, times by the top.
topics.teach: Explain how to find 3/5 of 40.
topics.talk: Ask her to find 3/4 of the bill when you next shop.

topics.title: Fractions, decimals and percentages
topics.hook: Per cent means “out of 100” (cent = 100, as in century).
topics.teach: Explain how to turn 3/5 into a percentage.
topics.talk: Which is better: 30% off or a third off?

topics.title: Percentages of amounts
topics.hook: Find 10% first (divide by 10), then build: 5% is half of it, 20% is double it.
topics.teach: Explain a quick way to find 15% of something.
topics.talk: Ask her to work out a 10% tip, then 15%.

topics.title: Order of operations
topics.hook: BIDMAS: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, Addition and Subtraction.
topics.teach: Explain why 3 + 4 × 2 is 11, not 14.
topics.talk: Ask her what 10 − 2 × 3 is.

topics.title: Algebra: substitution
topics.hook: 3a means 3 × a: swap the letter for its number, then use BIDMAS.
topics.teach: Explain what 3a means if a = 5.
topics.talk: If a = 4, is 2a the same as 24?

topics.title: Sequences and the nth term
topics.hook: The difference is the times table: 3, 5, 7, 9… goes up in 2s, so the nth term is 2n + 1.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between the term-to-term rule and the nth term.
topics.talk: What is the 100th term of 3, 5, 7, 9…?

topics.title: Solving equations
topics.hook: Keep the scales balanced: whatever you do to one side, do to the other.
topics.teach: Explain how you solve 3x + 5 = 20.
topics.talk: I think of a number, double it and add 3. I get 17. What was my number?

topics.title: Ratio and sharing
topics.hook: Add the parts, find one part, then multiply: 3 : 5 means 8 parts in all.
topics.teach: Explain how to share £40 in the ratio 3 : 5.
topics.talk: Share 12 sweets between you in the ratio 1 : 2.

topics.title: Factors, multiples and primes
topics.hook: A prime has exactly two factors, 1 and itself. So 1 isn’t prime, and 2 is the only even prime.
topics.teach: Explain why 51 is not a prime number.
topics.talk: Is 91 prime? (Try 7.)

topics.title: Angle facts
topics.hook: Straight line 180°, round a point 360°, triangle 180°, quadrilateral 360°.
topics.teach: Explain how you find a missing angle in a triangle.
topics.talk: Ask her what the angles in a triangle add up to.

topics.title: Long multiplication
topics.hook: Split one number into tens and ones, multiply each part, then add. Don’t forget the place-holder zero!
topics.teach: Explain how you work out 34 × 26 by splitting one of the numbers.
topics.talk: Ask her for 23 × 4 in her head, then 23 × 40.

topics.title: Long division and remainders
topics.hook: Does McDonald’s Sell Burgers? Divide, Multiply, Subtract, Bring down.
topics.teach: Explain when a remainder means you round UP and when it means you round down.
topics.talk: 7 friends share 50 sweets. How many each, and how many left?

topics.title: Area and perimeter
topics.hook: Area covers the inside (squares, cm²); perimeter is the fence around the edge (cm).
topics.teach: Explain the difference between area and perimeter, and why a triangle’s area is half base times height.
topics.talk: Guess the area of the kitchen table, then measure it.

topics.title: Volume of cuboids
topics.hook: Volume = length × width × height: how many cubes fill the box.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the volume of a shoebox.
topics.talk: How many 1 cm cubes would fit in a 10 cm cube?

topics.title: Coordinates in four quadrants
topics.hook: Along the corridor, then up the stairs: x first, then y.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to a point’s coordinates when you reflect it in the x-axis.
topics.talk: Play a quick game of Battleships with negative coordinates.

topics.title: Converting units
topics.hook: Kangaroos Hop Down Mountains Drinking Chocolate Milk: kilo, hecto, deca, metre, deci, centi, milli.
topics.teach: Explain how you change 2.3 km into metres, and why you multiply.
topics.talk: How many millilitres in the bottle in the fridge? How many litres is that?

topics.title: Time and timetables
topics.hook: After 12 noon, add 12 for the 24-hour clock: 3 pm is 15:00.
topics.teach: Explain how you work out how long it is from 09:45 to 11:20.
topics.talk: Next time you catch a bus or train, ask her to plan it from the timetable.

topics.title: Multi-step money problems
topics.hook: RUCSAC: Read, Understand, Choose, Solve, Answer, Check.
topics.teach: Explain how you decide what to work out first in a two-step problem.
topics.talk: At the shop: three of these and a £10 note, what’s the change?

topics.title: Probability
topics.hook: From 0 (impossible) to 1 (certain). The chance it does NOT happen = 1 − the chance it does.
topics.teach: Explain why the probability of an event and its opposite add up to 1.
topics.talk: Roll a dice 30 times together and compare the number of 6s with what she expected.

topics.title: Bar charts, pie charts and line graphs
topics.hook: A pie chart is a full turn: 360° shared out between the data.
topics.teach: Explain why a pie chart sector of 90° is a quarter of the data.
topics.talk: Find a chart in the news and ask her what it shows.

topics.title: Key facts
topics.hook: Know them instantly, like 5, 6, 7, 8 (56 = 7 × 8), and your brain is free for the hard part of a question.
topics.teach: Explain how you remember what the angles in a triangle add up to.
topics.talk: Quick-fire: what is 12 squared?

topics.title: Shapes and their properties
topics.hook: Quad means four: a quad bike has four wheels and a quadrilateral has four sides.
topics.intro: Mathematicians have exact names for shapes and their parts. Knowing them means you can describe any shape precisely.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a rhombus and a parallelogram.
topics.talk: Spot three different quadrilaterals around the house.

items.hook: Fill empty places with zeros to compare: 0.4 = 0.40, which beats 0.35.
items.example: Money: £0.40 is 40p and £0.35 is 35p, so 0.4 is bigger even though it has fewer digits.

items.hook: Subtracting a negative is adding: 5 − (−3) = 5 + 3 = 8.
items.example: Lift buttons: from floor −2 (the car park) go up 5 floors and you reach floor 3. A thermometer works the same way.
A fuel gauge: the needle at 3/4 means the tank is three quarters full.
Would you rather share a pizza between 5 people or 8? Each 1/5 is a bigger slice than each 1/8.
Half a dozen eggs is 6 out of 12: 6/12 = 1/2, the same amount with a different name.
Half a pizza plus a third of a pizza: cut both into sixths, 3/6 + 2/6 = 5/6.

items.hook: “Of” means ×: half of a quarter = 1/2 × 1/4 = 1/8.
items.example: Half of a quarter of a cake is an eighth of the cake.

items.hook: To make a percentage, make the bottom 100: 3/5 = 60/100 = 60%.
items.example: A phone battery showing 50% is half full; 25% is a quarter full.
Shop sale: 15% off a £40 jumper is £4 + £2 = £6 off, so you pay £34.

items.hook: D and M are a team, and so are A and S: do each pair from left to right.
items.example: 3 drinks at £2 plus a £4 sandwich: 4 + 3 × 2 = £10, not £14.
A phone plan costs £5 plus £2 per GB: 5 + 2g. Using 3 GB costs 5 + 2 × 3 = £11.
Tables pushed together in a row: 1 table seats 4 and each extra table adds 2 seats, so n tables seat 2n + 2.

items.hook: Undo it backwards: for 3x + 5 = 20, take away 5 first, then divide by 3.
items.example: Cinema: 3 tickets plus £5 of popcorn cost £35. 3t + 5 = 35, so each ticket is £10.
Squash: 1 part cordial to 4 parts water. A 500 ml jug needs 100 ml of cordial and 400 ml of water.

items.hook: Factors fit into a number; multiples are in its times table. Factors are few, multiples go on for ever.
items.example: Some cicadas in North America only come out every 13 or 17 years: prime numbers!

items.hook: A cute little angle is acute (under 90°); obtuse is between 90° and 180°; reflex is more than 180°.
items.example: Clock hands at 3 o’clock make a right angle (90°); at 6 o’clock they make a straight line (180°).
A theatre with 26 rows of 34 seats: 34 × 20 = 680 and 34 × 6 = 204, so 884 seats.

items.hook: Remainders: round UP when everyone needs a place (buses); round DOWN when only full ones count (bags).
items.example: 50 pupils in 16-seat minibuses need 4 buses, but 50 sweets in bags of 16 fill only 3 bags.

items.hook: A triangle is half the rectangle around it: ½ × base × height.
items.example: Carpet is sold by area (m²); a fence is sold by length, so for that you need the perimeter.
A 10 cm × 10 cm × 10 cm box holds 1000 cm³, which is exactly 1 litre: a big carton of juice.
Battleships and map grid references both go across first, then up.

items.hook: Changing to a smaller unit? Multiply (you need more of them). To a bigger unit? Divide.
items.example: A 5 km fun run is 5000 m; a 2 litre bottle of squash holds 2000 ml.

items.hook: Count on in hops: up to the next o’clock, then whole hours, then the minutes left.
items.example: Train timetables: 14:45 to 16:10 is 15 min + 1 h + 10 min = 1 h 25 min.
3 comics at £2.75 each from a £10 note: £8.25 spent, so £1.75 change.
A weather app showing a 70% chance of rain means a 30% chance of staying dry.

items.hook: Degrees for one item = 360 ÷ total × that item’s number.
items.example: In a class of 30, each child gets 12° of the pie chart (360 ÷ 30 = 12).

items.prompt: What is 7²?
items.explain: What is 7²: 49.
items.hook: Squared means times itself: 7² = 7 × 7, not 7 × 2.
items.example: A square patio 7 tiles by 7 tiles uses 49 tiles.

items.prompt: What is 9²?
items.explain: What is 9²: 81.
items.hook: In the 9 times table the digits add to 9: 8 + 1 = 9.

items.prompt: What is 12²?
items.explain: What is 12²: 144.
items.hook: A dozen dozen is a gross: 12 × 12 = 144.
items.example: Twelve boxes of a dozen eggs make 144 eggs.

items.prompt: What is 15²?
items.explain: What is 15²: 225.
items.hook: Squaring a number ending in 5: 1 × 2 = 2, then write 25 after it, giving 225.

items.prompt: What is √64?
items.explain: What is √64: 8.
items.hook: Square root asks “what times ITSELF makes this?” 8 × 8 = 64.
items.example: A chessboard is 8 squares by 8 squares: 64 squares in all.

items.prompt: What is √121?
items.explain: What is √121: 11.
items.hook: 11 × 11 = 121, a number that reads the same backwards.

items.prompt: What is {{1/8}} as a decimal?
items.explain: What is {{1/8}} as a decimal: 0.125.

items.prompt: What is {{3/4}} as a percentage?
items.explain: What is {{3/4}} as a percentage: 75%.
items.hook: Think coins: 3/4 of £1 is 75p, which is 75 out of 100.
items.example: Three quarters of an hour is 45 minutes; three quarters of £1 is 75p.

items.prompt: What is {{1/5}} as a decimal?
items.explain: What is {{1/5}} as a decimal: 0.2.

items.prompt: What is 0.05 as a percentage?
items.explain: What is 0.05 as a percentage: 5%.
items.hook: Decimal to percentage: multiply by 100. 0.05 × 100 = 5%.
items.example: 5p is 0.05 of a pound, which is 5%.

items.prompt: How many metres are in 1 kilometre?
items.explain: How many metres are in 1 kilometre: 1000.
items.hook: Kilo means a thousand: a kilometre is 1000 metres, a kilogram 1000 grams.
items.example: A kilometre is two and a half laps of a 400 m running track.

items.prompt: How many millilitres are in 1 litre?
items.explain: How many millilitres are in 1 litre: 1000.
items.hook: Milli means a thousandth: a millilitre is a thousandth of a litre.
items.example: A 1 litre carton of juice fills four 250 ml glasses.

items.prompt: How many grams are in 1 kilogram?
items.explain: How many grams are in 1 kilogram: 1000.
items.example: A 1 kg bag of sugar holds 1000 grams.

items.prompt: How many centimetres are in 1 metre?
items.explain: How many centimetres are in 1 metre: 100.
items.hook: Centi means a hundredth, like a century is 100 years.
items.example: A metre stick has 100 cm marked on it.

items.prompt: What do the angles in a triangle add up to?
items.explain: What do the angles in a triangle add up to: 180°.
items.hook: Tear the three corners off a paper triangle: they fit together on a straight line, 180°.

items.prompt: What do the angles around a point add up to?
items.explain: What do the angles around a point add up to: 360°.
items.hook: A full turn is 360°.
items.example: A skateboarder who does a “three-sixty” spins all the way round.

items.prompt: What do the angles in a quadrilateral add up to?
items.explain: What do the angles in a quadrilateral add up to: 360°.
items.hook: A diagonal cuts a quadrilateral into two triangles: 2 × 180° = 360°.

items.prompt: What is the smallest prime number?
items.explain: What is the smallest prime number: 2.
items.hook: 1 is not prime (it has only one factor). 2 is the smallest prime and the only even one.

items.prompt: What is an acute angle?
items.explain: What is an acute angle: less than 90°.
items.hook: A cute little angle: acute angles are small, less than 90°.
items.example: The tip of a slice of pizza makes an acute angle.

items.prompt: What is an obtuse angle?
items.explain: What is an obtuse angle: between 90° and 180°.
items.hook: Obtuse is open wide: more than a square corner, less than a straight line.
items.example: A laptop screen tipped back past upright makes an obtuse angle.

items.prompt: How many sides does a hexagon have?
items.explain: How many sides does a hexagon have: 6.
items.hook: Hexagon and six both have an x.
items.example: The cells in a honeycomb are hexagons.

items.prompt: How many sides does an octagon have?
items.explain: How many sides does an octagon have: 8.
items.hook: An octopus has eight arms; an octagon has eight sides.
items.example: A UK STOP sign is an octagon.

items.prompt: What is the formula for the area of a rectangle?
items.explain: What is the formula for the area of a rectangle: length × width.
items.hook: Count the squares: rows × columns, so length × width.

items.prompt: What is the formula for the area of a triangle?
items.explain: What is the formula for the area of a triangle: ½ × base × height.
items.hook: A triangle is half of a rectangle: ½ × base × height.

items.prompt: Which quadrilateral has two pairs of parallel sides and all sides equal, but no right angles?
items.explain: A rhombus is a “pushed-over square”: four equal sides, opposite angles equal.
items.hook: A rhombus is a squashed square: four equal sides.
items.example: The diamond on a playing card is a rhombus.

items.prompt: Which quadrilateral has exactly one pair of parallel sides?
items.explain: Trapezium: one pair of parallel sides. Parallelogram: two pairs.
items.hook: Trapezium: ONE pair of parallel sides. Parallelogram: two pairs (“parallel” is in its name).
items.example: A bucket or a classic handbag seen from the side is a trapezium shape.

items.prompt: Which quadrilateral has two pairs of equal sides that are next to each other, like a diamond on a string?
items.explain: A kite’s equal sides are adjacent (touching), not opposite.
items.hook: A kite: two short sides together at the top, two long sides together at the bottom.

items.prompt: What is a triangle with all three sides equal called?
items.explain: Equilateral: all sides equal, all angles 60°.
items.hook: Equi-lateral = equal sides: all three the same.
items.example: The triangle used to rack up snooker balls is equilateral.

items.prompt: What is a triangle with exactly two equal sides called?
items.explain: Isosceles: two equal sides and two equal base angles.
items.hook: Isosceles is Greek for “equal legs”: two equal sides.

items.prompt: What is a triangle with no equal sides called?
items.explain: Scalene: all sides and all angles different.
items.hook: Scalene comes from the Greek for “uneven”: no sides the same.

items.prompt: What is the distance from the centre of a circle to its edge called?
items.explain: Radius: centre to edge. Diameter: edge to edge through the centre, twice the radius.
items.hook: The radius goes halfway across; the diameter goes all the way and is double.
items.example: A bicycle spoke runs from the hub towards the rim, like a radius.

items.prompt: What is the distance all the way round a circle called?
items.explain: The circumference is a circle’s perimeter. It is about 3.14 (π) times the diameter.
items.hook: Circum means around, as in circumnavigate (to sail around the world).
items.example: The ribbon around a birthday cake measures its circumference.

items.prompt: A circle has a radius of 7 cm. What is its diameter?
items.explain: The diameter is twice the radius: 2 × 7 = 14 cm.
items.hook: Diameter is double the radius: d = 2r.
items.example: A pizza’s size is measured across the middle: its diameter.

items.prompt: What is a 2D shape with all sides equal and all angles equal called?
items.explain: A square is a regular quadrilateral; an equilateral triangle is a regular triangle.
items.hook: Regular means everything matches: all sides AND all angles equal.
items.example: A square and a STOP sign (a regular octagon) are regular polygons.

items.prompt: What is the flat pattern that folds up to make a 3D shape called?
items.explain: A cube’s net is six squares joined so they fold into a box.
items.hook: A net is the shape’s flat-pack: fold it up to build the 3D shape.
items.example: Unfold a cereal box and the flat card is a net of a cuboid.

items.prompt: How many faces, edges and vertices does a cube have?
items.explain: Count them on a dice: 6 faces, 12 edges where faces meet, 8 corners (vertices).
items.hook: Check with Euler: faces + vertices − edges = 2. For a cube, 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

items.prompt: Which 3D shape has two circular faces and one curved surface?
items.explain: A cylinder is like a tin of beans: two flat circles and a curved side.
items.example: Tins of beans, drinks cans and toilet-roll tubes are cylinders.

items.prompt: Which 3D shape has a square base and four triangular faces meeting at a point?
items.explain: The pyramids of Giza are square-based pyramids.
items.hook: A pyramid is named after its base: square base, square-based pyramid.

items.prompt: Two shapes are exactly the same shape and size. What word describes them?
items.explain: Congruent shapes fit exactly on top of each other, even if one is turned or flipped.
items.hook: Congruent = identical twins: same shape AND same size. Similar = same shape, different size.
items.example: Stamps from the same sheet are congruent.

items.prompt: What is the name for lines that are always the same distance apart and never meet?
items.explain: Parallel lines, like railway tracks. Perpendicular lines meet at a right angle.
items.hook: The two l’s in the middle of paraLLel are a pair of parallel lines.
items.example: Railway tracks and the lines on writing paper are parallel.

items.prompt: What is the name for two lines that meet at a right angle?
items.explain: Perpendicular: at 90° to each other, like the corner of a page.
items.hook: Perpendicular lines make a perfect L or T: a right angle.
items.example: The corner where a wall meets the floor is perpendicular.

items.prompt: How many lines of symmetry does a regular hexagon have?
items.explain: A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides.
items.hook: A regular polygon has as many lines of symmetry as it has sides.
items.example: A snowflake usually has six lines of symmetry.
